title: Anthrobots self-organize into discrete, stable movement types with individual fingerprints

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Anthrobots self-organize into discrete, stable movement types with individual fingerprints

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Because Anthrobot movement types are highly consistent and rarely interconvert (for example between circular and linear), the authors conclude that Anthrobots self-organize into discrete, stable movement types, each bot having a distinct motility fingerprint.

fields.label: Work
fields.value: Motile Living Biobots Self-Construct from Adult Human Somatic Progenitor Seed Cells

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Gumuskaya G 2024, Motile Living Biobots Self-Construct from Adult Human Somatic Progenitor Seed Cells › Results › Anthrobots Self‐Organize into Discrete Movement Types

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: The fact that Anthrobots exhibit movement types with high “consistency” and low rates of inter‐type conversion (e.g., between circulars and linear) suggests that Anthrobots self‐organize into discrete and stable movement types, each bot having a distinct motility fingerprint.

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Gumuskaya G, Srivastava P, Cooper BG, Lesser H, Semegran B, Garnier S, Levin M, “Motile Living Biobots Self-Construct from Adult Human Somatic Progenitor Seed Cells”, Advanced science (Weinheim, Baden-Wurttemberg, Germany) (2024), doi:10.1002/advs.202303575; section “Results › Anthrobots Self‐Organize into Discrete Movement Types”. Scope: NHBE-derived Anthrobots in vitro

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on levin-2024-anthrobots-11: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.68

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Consistency and interconversion are measurable, but discreteness and individual fingerprints are stronger interpretations. Existing trajectories can test short-term persistence but not a durable intrinsic identity.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Compare within-bot and between-bot movement-state consistency over time and test whether discrete-state models predict held-out trajectories better than continuous alternatives.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Motility fingerprint is not defined independently of the clustering procedure.

Five-hour recordings do not establish long-term stability.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
data adequacy: 0.58
analysis feasibility: 0.84
operationalizability: 0.74
data existence: 0.68
discriminating power: 0.58

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Within-bot consistency is measurable from the same five-hour tracks as the transition matrix, and those tracks are not public. Even with them, rare switching would not show that bots self-organize into types rather than simply keeping the geometry they had when recording started. The stability half is waiting on data; the self-organization wording stays underdetermined.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: For each bot, compute the fraction of its 30-second segments that stay in one movement class and the rate of switches between circular and linear. High within-bot consistency and rare cross-class switches would support stable individual types; frequent switching by the same bot would refute a lasting fingerprint. Separating active self-organization from a type fixed by the initial cilia pattern needs early-time tracks the consistency score alone does not provide.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
A fingerprint is only as discrete as the upstream cluster boundaries.

Per-bot identity of segments is not in a public file.

Low switching does not distinguish self-organization from a type fixed at release by cilia geometry.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
discriminating power: 0.34
operationalizability: 0.68
data existence: 0.15
data adequacy: 0.14
analysis feasibility: 0.18
